8. Akusalacchedanapañha 8. Question on Cutting Off Unwholesome States

“Bhante nāgasena, tathāgato sabbaṁ akusalaṁ jhāpetvā sabbaññutaṁ patto, udāhu sāvasese akusale sabbaññutaṁ patto”ti? “Venerable Nāgasena, did the Tathāgata attain omniscience after burning up all unwholesome states, or did he attain omniscience while some unwholesome states remained?” “Sabbaṁ, mahārāja, akusalaṁ jhāpetvā bhagavā sabbaññutaṁ patto, natthi bhagavato sesakaṁ akusalan”ti. “Your majesty, the Blessed One attained omniscience after burning up all unwholesome states. No unwholesome state remained in the Blessed One.”

“Kiṁ pana, bhante, dukkhā vedanā tathāgatassa kāye uppannapubbā”ti? “But, venerable sir, did painful feeling ever arise in the Tathāgata’s body?” “Āma, mahārāja, rājagahe bhagavato pādo sakalikāya khato, lohitapakkhandikābādho uppanno, kāye abhisanne jīvakena vireko kārito, vātābādhe uppanne upaṭṭhākena therena uṇhodakaṁ pariyiṭṭhan”ti. “Yes, your majesty. At Rājagaha the Blessed One’s foot was pierced by a splinter, and an illness involving bloody discharge (dysentery) arose. When his body was congested, Jīvaka administered a purgative. When a wind ailment arose, the elder who was his attendant (Ānanda) sought out hot water.”

“Yadi, bhante nāgasena, tathāgato sabbaṁ akusalaṁ jhāpetvā sabbaññutaṁ patto, tena hi bhagavato pādo sakalikāya khato, lohitapakkhandikā ca ābādho uppannoti yaṁ vacanaṁ, taṁ micchā. “Venerable Nāgasena, if the Tathāgata attained omniscience after burning up all unwholesome states, then the statement that the Blessed One’s foot was pierced by a splinter and that he suffered an illness with bloody discharge is false. Yadi tathāgatassa pādo sakalikāya khato, lohitapakkhandikā ca ābādho uppanno, tena hi tathāgato sabbaṁ akusalaṁ jhāpetvā sabbaññutaṁ pattoti tampi vacanaṁ micchā. But if the Tathāgata’s foot were pierced by a splinter and he suffered an illness with bloody discharge, then the statement that the Tathāgata attained omniscience after burning up all unwholesome states is also false. Natthi, bhante, vinā kammena vedayitaṁ, sabbaṁ taṁ vedayitaṁ kammamūlakaṁ, taṁ kammeneva vedayati, ayampi ubhato koṭiko pañho tavānuppatto, so tayā nibbāhitabbo”ti. Venerable sir, there is no experiencing of feeling without kamma; all feeling is rooted in kamma, and one feels it by way of kamma alone. This two-horned dilemma has now come to you, and it must be resolved by you.”

“Na hi, mahārāja, sabbaṁ taṁ vedayitaṁ kammamūlakaṁ. “Certainly not, your majesty; not all feeling is rooted in kamma. Aṭṭhahi, mahārāja, kāraṇehi vedayitāni uppajjanti, yehi kāraṇehi puthū sattā vedanā vediyanti. Feelings arise from eight causes, and by these causes many beings experience feeling. Katamehi aṭṭhahi? From which eight? Vātasamuṭṭhānānipi kho, mahārāja, idhekaccāni vedayitāni uppajjanti, Some feelings that arise here, your majesty, originate from wind; pittasamuṭṭhānānipi kho, mahārāja …pe… some, your majesty, from bile; ... semhasamuṭṭhānānipi kho, mahārāja …pe… some, your majesty, from phlegm; ... sannipātikānipi kho, mahārāja …pe… some, your majesty, from the combination of the three; ... utupariṇāmajānipi kho, mahārāja …pe… some, your majesty, from the change of seasons; ... visamaparihārajānipi kho, mahārāja …pe… some, your majesty, from careless conduct; ... opakkamikānipi kho, mahārāja …pe… some, your majesty, from external assault; ... kammavipākajānipi kho, mahārāja, idhekaccāni vedayitāni uppajjanti. and some, your majesty, arise from the result of kamma. Imehi kho, mahārāja, aṭṭhahi kāraṇehi puthū sattā vedanā vedayanti. By these eight causes many beings experience feeling. Tattha ye te puggalā ‘satte kammaṁ vibādhatī’ti vadeyyuṁ, te ime puggalā sattakāraṇaṁ paṭibāhanti. Among these, those people who say ‘kamma afflicts beings’ are denying the other causes that exist for beings. Tesaṁ taṁ vacanaṁ micchā”ti. Their statement is false.” “Bhante nāgasena, yañca vātikaṁ yañca pittikaṁ yañca semhikaṁ yañca sannipātikaṁ yañca utupariṇāmajaṁ yañca visamaparihārajaṁ yañca opakkamikaṁ, sabbete kammasamuṭṭhānāyeva, kammeneva te sabbe sambhavantī”ti. “Venerable Nāgasena, whatever is caused by wind, bile, phlegm, the combination of the three, the change of seasons, uneven conduct, or external assault: all of these originate from kamma alone. All of them come to be by way of kamma.”

“Yadi, mahārāja, tepi sabbe kammasamuṭṭhānāva ābādhā bhaveyyuṁ, na tesaṁ koṭṭhāsato lakkhaṇāni bhaveyyuṁ. “Your majesty, if all those ailments originated from kamma alone, they would not have distinct characteristics by category. Vāto kho, mahārāja, kuppamāno dasavidhena kuppati sītena uṇhena jighacchāya pipāsāya atibhuttena ṭhānena padhānena ādhāvanena upakkamena kammavipākena. Wind, your majesty, is aggravated in ten ways: by cold, by heat, by hunger, by thirst, by overeating, by standing, by exertion, by violent motion, by assault, and by the result of kamma. Tatra ye te nava vidhā, na te atīte, na anāgate, vattamānake bhave uppajjanti, tasmā na vattabbā ‘kammasambhavā sabbā vedanā’ti. Of these, the nine kinds do not arise in the past or the future, but in the present existence. Therefore it should not be said that ‘all feeling originates from kamma.’ Pittaṁ, mahārāja, kuppamānaṁ tividhena kuppati sītena uṇhena visamabhojanena. Bile, your majesty, is aggravated in three ways: by cold, by heat, and by unsuitable food. Semhaṁ, mahārāja, kuppamānaṁ tividhena kuppati sītena uṇhena annapānena. Phlegm, your majesty, is aggravated in three ways: by cold, by heat, and by food and drink. Yo ca, mahārāja, vāto yañca pittaṁ yañca semhaṁ, tehi tehi kopehi kuppitvā missī hutvā sakaṁ sakaṁ vedanaṁ ākaḍḍhati. And the wind, the bile, and the phlegm, having been aggravated by their respective disturbances and having become mixed, bring on their own particular feeling. Utupariṇāmajā, mahārāja, vedanā utupariṇāmena uppajjati. Feeling born of the change of seasons arises through the change of seasons. Visamaparihārajā vedanā visamaparihārena uppajjati. Feeling born of uneven conduct arises through uneven conduct. Opakkamikā, mahārāja, vedanā atthi kiriyā, atthi kammavipākā, kammavipākajā vedanā pubbe katena kammena uppajjati. As for feeling from external assault, your majesty, there is that which is mere action and there is that which is the result of kamma. Feeling born of the result of kamma arises through kamma done in the past. Iti kho, mahārāja, appaṁ kammavipākajaṁ, bahutaraṁ avasesaṁ. Thus, your majesty, what is born of the result of kamma is small, and what remains is far greater. Tattha bālā ‘sabbaṁ kammavipākajaṁ yevā’ti atidhāvanti. In this matter fools overreach, saying, ‘It is all the result of kamma.’ Taṁ kammaṁ na sakkā vinā buddhañāṇena vavatthānaṁ kātuṁ. That kamma cannot be determined without the knowledge of a Buddha.

Yaṁ pana, mahārāja, bhagavato pādo sakalikāya khato, taṁ vedayitaṁ neva vātasamuṭṭhānaṁ, na pittasamuṭṭhānaṁ, na semhasamuṭṭhānaṁ, na sannipātikaṁ, na utupariṇāmajaṁ, na visamaparihārajaṁ, na kammavipākajaṁ, opakkamikaṁyeva. As for the splinter that pierced the Blessed One’s foot, your majesty, that feeling was not born of wind, nor of bile, nor of phlegm, nor of their combination, nor of the change of seasons, nor of uneven conduct, nor of the result of kamma. It was from external assault alone. Devadatto hi, mahārāja, bahūni jātisatasahassāni tathāgate āghātaṁ bandhi, so tena āghātena mahatiṁ garuṁ silaṁ gahetvā ‘matthake pātessāmī’ti muñci, athaññe dve selā āgantvā taṁ silaṁ tathāgataṁ asampattaṁyeva sampaṭicchiṁsu, tāsaṁ pahārena papaṭikā bhijjitvā bhagavato pāde patitvā ruhiraṁ uppādesi, kammavipākato vā, mahārāja, bhagavato esā vedanā nibbattā kiriyato vā, tatuddhaṁ natthaññā vedanā. For Devadatta, your majesty, bore a grudge against the Tathāgata for many hundreds of thousands of births. Out of that grudge he took up a great, heavy rock and let it go, thinking, ‘I will drop it on his head.’ Then two other rocks came and caught that rock before it reached the Tathāgata. By the force of the impact a splinter broke off, fell on the Blessed One’s foot, and drew blood. This feeling of the Blessed One, your majesty, was produced either from the result of kamma or from mere action; beyond these there is no other feeling.

Yathā, mahārāja, khettaduṭṭhatāya vā bījaṁ na sambhavati bījaduṭṭhatāya vā; Just as, your majesty, a seed fails to grow because either the field or the seed is faulty, evameva kho, mahārāja, kammavipākato vā bhagavato esā vedanā nibbattā kiriyato vā, tatuddhaṁ natthaññā vedanā. in the same way this feeling of the Blessed One was produced either from the result of kamma or from mere action; beyond these there is no other feeling.

Yathā vā pana, mahārāja, koṭṭhaduṭṭhatāya vā bhojanaṁ visamaṁ pariṇamati āhāraduṭṭhatāya vā; Or again, your majesty, just as food is digested badly because either the stomach or the food is faulty, evameva kho, mahārāja, kammavipākato vā bhagavato esā vedanā nibbattā kiriyato vā, tatuddhaṁ natthaññā vedanā. so too this feeling of the Blessed One was produced either from the result of kamma or from mere action; beyond these there is no other feeling. Api ca, mahārāja, natthi bhagavato kammavipākajā vedanā, natthi visamaparihārajā vedanā, avasesehi samuṭṭhānehi bhagavato vedanā uppajjati, tāya ca pana vedanāya na sakkā bhagavantaṁ jīvitā voropetuṁ. Moreover, your majesty, the Blessed One has no feeling born of the result of kamma, and none born of uneven conduct. The Blessed One’s feeling arises from the remaining causes, and by such feeling it is not possible to deprive the Blessed One of life.

Nipatanti, mahārāja, imasmiṁ cātumahābhūtike kāye iṭṭhāniṭṭhā subhāsubhavedanā. Pleasant and unpleasant, agreeable and disagreeable feelings, your majesty, fall upon this body made of the four great elements. Idha, mahārāja, ākāse khitto leḍḍu mahāpathaviyā nipatati, api nu kho so, mahārāja, leḍḍu pubbe katena mahāpathaviyā nipatī”ti? Suppose, your majesty, a clod thrown into the air falls on the great earth. Does that clod fall on the great earth because of something done in the past?” “Na hi, bhante, natthi so, bhante, hetu mahāpathaviyā, yena hetunā mahāpathavī kusalākusalavipākaṁ paṭisaṁvedeyya, paccuppannena, bhante, akammakena hetunā so leḍḍu mahāpathaviyaṁ nipatati”. “Certainly not, venerable sir. There is no cause in the great earth by which the great earth would experience the result of wholesome or unwholesome deeds. The clod falls on the great earth by a present cause, one not rooted in kamma.” “Yathā, mahārāja, mahāpathavī, evaṁ tathāgato daṭṭhabbo. “Just as the great earth, your majesty, so should the Tathāgata be regarded. Yathā leḍḍu pubbe akatena mahāpathaviyaṁ nipatati; As the clod falls on the great earth without anything done in the past, evameva kho, mahārāja, tathāgatassa pubbe akatena sā sakalikā pāde nipatitā. in the same way, your majesty, that splinter fell on the Tathāgata’s foot without anything done in the past.

Idha pana, mahārāja, manussā mahāpathaviṁ bhindanti ca khaṇanti ca, api nu kho, mahārāja, te manussā pubbe katena mahāpathaviṁ bhindanti ca khaṇanti cā”ti? Again, your majesty, people break up and dig the great earth. Do those people break up and dig the great earth because of something done in the past?” “Na hi, bhante”ti. “Certainly not, venerable sir.” “Evameva kho, mahārāja, yā sā sakalikā bhagavato pāde nipatitā, na sā sakalikā pubbe katena bhagavato pāde nipatitā. “In the same way, your majesty, the splinter that fell on the Blessed One’s foot did not fall because of something done in the past. Yopi, mahārāja, bhagavato lohitapakkhandikābādho uppanno, sopi ābādho na pubbe katena uppanno, sannipātikeneva uppanno, ye keci, mahārāja, bhagavato kāyikā ābādhā uppannā, na te kammābhinibbattā, channaṁ etesaṁ samuṭṭhānānaṁ aññatarato nibbattā. And the illness with bloody discharge that arose in the Blessed One did not arise because of the past either. It arose from the combination of the humours alone. Whatever bodily ailments arose in the Blessed One, your majesty, were not produced by kamma. They were produced from one or another of these six causes.

Bhāsitampetaṁ, mahārāja, bhagavatā devātidevena saṁyuttanikāyavaralañchake moḷiyasīvake veyyākaraṇe—And this too was said, your majesty, by the Blessed One, the god above the gods, in the Moḷiyasīvaka explanation, in the excellent collection of the Saṃyutta Nikāya:

‘Pittasamuṭṭhānānipi kho, sīvaka, idhekaccāni vedayitāni uppajjanti. ‘Some feelings that arise here, Sīvaka, originate from bile. Sāmampi kho etaṁ, sīvaka, veditabbaṁ, yathā pittasamuṭṭhānānipi idhekaccāni vedayitāni uppajjanti. This is something to be known by oneself, Sīvaka, that some feelings arise originating from bile. Lokassapi kho etaṁ, sīvaka, saccasammataṁ, yathā pittasamuṭṭhānānipi idhekaccāni vedayitāni uppajjanti. It is also accepted as true in the world, Sīvaka, that some feelings arise originating from bile. Tatra, sīvaka, ye te samaṇabrāhmaṇā evaṁvādino evaṁdiṭṭhino “yaṁ kiñcāyaṁ purisapuggalo paṭisaṁvedeti sukhaṁ vā dukkhaṁ vā adukkhamasukhaṁ vā, sabbaṁ taṁ pubbe katahetū”ti. Now, Sīvaka, those ascetics and brahmins who hold this doctrine and view, “Whatever this person experiences, whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant, all of that is caused by past action,” Yañca sāmaṁ ñātaṁ, tañca atidhāvanti, yañca loke saccasammataṁ, tañca atidhāvanti. overreach what they know by themselves, and they overreach what is accepted as true in the world. Tasmā tesaṁ samaṇabrāhmaṇānaṁ micchāti vadāmi. Therefore I say that these ascetics and brahmins are wrong.

Semhasamuṭṭhānānipi kho, sīvaka, idhekaccāni vedayitāni uppajjanti. Some feelings that arise here, Sīvaka, originate from phlegm; ... Vātasamuṭṭhānānipi kho, sīvaka …pe… some, Sīvaka, originate from wind; ... sannipātikānipi kho, sīvaka …pe… some, Sīvaka, from the combination of the three ; ... utupariṇāmajānipi kho, sīvaka …pe… some, Sīvaka, from the change of seasons; ... visamaparihārajānipi kho, sīvaka …pe… some, Sīvaka, from uneven conduct; ... opakkamikānipi kho, sīvaka …pe… some, Sīvaka, from external assault; ... kammavipākajānipi kho, sīvaka, idhekaccāni vedayitāni uppajjanti. and some feelings that arise here, Sīvaka, are born of the result of kamma. Sāmampi kho etaṁ, sīvaka, veditabbaṁ, yathā kammavipākajānipi idhekaccāni vedayitāni uppajjanti. This is something to be known by oneself, Sīvaka, that some feelings arise born of the result of kamma. Lokassapi kho etaṁ, sīvaka, saccasammataṁ, yathā kammavipākajānipi idhekaccāni vedayitāni uppajjanti. It is also accepted as true in the world, Sīvaka, that some feelings arise born of the result of kamma. Tatra, sīvaka, ye te samaṇabrāhmaṇā evaṁvādino evaṁdiṭṭhino “yaṁ kiñcāyaṁ purisapuggalo paṭisaṁvedeti sukhaṁ vā dukkhaṁ vā adukkhamasukhaṁ vā, sabbaṁ taṁ pubbe katahetū”ti. Now, Sīvaka, those ascetics and brahmins who hold this doctrine and view, “Whatever this person experiences, whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant, all of that is caused by past action,” Yañca sāmaṁ ñātaṁ, tañca atidhāvanti, yañca loke saccasammataṁ, tañca atidhāvanti. overreach what they know by themselves, and they overreach what is accepted as true in the world. Tasmā tesaṁ samaṇabrāhmaṇānaṁ micchāti vadāmī’ti. Therefore I say that these ascetics and brahmins are wrong.’

Itipi, mahārāja, na sabbā vedanā kammavipākajā, sabbaṁ, mahārāja, akusalaṁ jhāpetvā bhagavā sabbaññutaṁ pattoti evametaṁ dhārehī”ti. So too, your majesty, not all feeling is born of the result of kamma. Hold this firmly: the Blessed One attained omniscience after burning up all unwholesome states.” “Sādhu, bhante nāgasena, evametaṁ tathā sampaṭicchāmī”ti. “Very good, Venerable Nāgasena. I accept it as you say.”

Akusalacchedanapañho aṭṭhamo. Question on Cutting Off Unwholesome States eighth
